speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKER'S GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF CEYLON, MADAME BANDARANAIKE
speechtext: It gives me much pleasure to bring to the attention of hon. members the presence in the Speaker's gallery of a very distinguished visitor to our country, Madame Bandaranaike, Prime Minister of Ceylon.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKER'S GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF CEYLON, MADAME BANDARANAIKE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKER'S GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF CEYLON, MADAME BANDARANAIKE
speechtext:
Mrs. Bandaranaike heads the government of a country with which, over a long period of years, we have had very close ties. We welcome you, Madame Prime Minister, as the enlightened leader of a country with which we are associated as partners in the Commonwealth of Nations and we welcome you as a friend of Canada.
On behalf of hon. members I thank you for the hospitality which your parliament, your government and you personally have extended to Canadian parliamentarians who have visited Ceylon through the Inter-Parliamentary Union and the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association.

We are therefore very happy to welcome you to Canada. On behalf of hon. members and all Canadians, I want to wish you and those who came with you a useful as well as a pleasant visit in Canada.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKER'S GALLERY OF PRIME MINISTER OF CEYLON, MADAME BANDARANAIKE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: AIRCRAFT PURCHASED FOR TESTING FLYING POTENTIAL OF PILOT TRAINEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for asking this question. The CBC report last night by Mr. Cleverley was erroneous in six major respects. The government acquired the aircraft in 1970 not for $1,500 above list price but for $1,500 below. The air force trainers have always been painted yellow, rather than only during World War II. The immediate predecessor of this aircraft, for example, was painted yellow. The aircraft, as used as part of the air force training, is used for aerobatic training in the sense of doing crisis control, stalls, spins and so on. It is for that reason that the aircraft whose manufacturer I take it was probably the source of the CBC reporter's information was not accepted and this aircraft was. The aerobatic procedures which are used are not the same as those in the United States air force. The Americans follow a different and more expensive system. We think ours is the better. The aircraft are not used for 12 hours flying as asserted but for 20 hours. As I have already indicated, we follow a different system in order to bring our pilots at an earlier point to a more advanced stage. I think it will be recognized that the CBC was again spreading false news.

Apparently, it is considered that this expenditure does not carry the same risk as an expenditure on mining assets. However, all these expenditures bear the same degree of risk, which is contingent upon whether the mine has the ability to produce profitably. In my opinion, these points should be taken into consideration when amending the bill. In dropping the three-year exemption in favour of an accelerated depreciation, the government has definitely reduced the incentive to risk money in mining and presumably feels that risk capital, as in the past, has been getting off too lightly in the tax structure.
Turning now to the wiping out of depreciation allowances of 33-1/3 per cent by substituting $1 credit for every $3 worth of exploration, the government has again departed from the standard type of tax incentives that are offered around the world. The United States has continued to offer percentage depletion at varying rates based on the gross revenue from mining, with a maximum deduction of 50 per cent of the net income before depletion. In the United States, for example, after exhaustive hearings on the subject, Congress substantially maintained the existing levels for hard minerals.
Around the world, most countries are not reducing tax incentives to promote mining exploration and development. The depletion allowance of 33-1/3 per cent was allowed on the presumption that mining was a wasting resource and that allowance should be made for this in order to encourage new discoveries and development. While there may be considerable argument over the best way to give incentive to the mining industry, depletion allowances of fixed percentages seem to have worked well in Canada.
Under Bill C-259, companies not engaged on off-property mineral rights exploration will receive no depletion allowance at all. While superficially this may seem to encourage mineral exploration, on closer analysis it is highly discriminatory and fails to meet the condition for which the depletion allowance was instituted. Some mining companies are by nature better organized and committed to broad and continuing mineral exploration. Others are concerned only with metals, such as gold, asbestos, potash and iron ore, of which abundant supplies and reserves are known to exist.
For some minerals there may be no point in continuing exploration programs. It seems a fundamental error and wholly unwarranted to make the depletion allowance completely dependent on future exploration expenditures. The justification for depletion allowance is the wasting asset nature of mining and ore bodies. There is no doubt that at the present time the depletion allowance has been an important factor in enabling Canadian companies to sell their products on the world market.
In the matter of earned depletion, the bill seems to need broadening so as to include the cost of any exploration and development in the vicinity of an existing mine, the development of permanent underground fixtures and development costs related to a major expansion of an open pit mine.

In the area of new processing facilities that have to do with the processing of Canadian ores beyond the stage to which they were previously processed in Canada, it would seem logical that all new facilities should qualify if it is our intention to increase the processing of ores in Canada. This would seem to be a desirable role for Canada, one that would meet with wide approval.
The announcement by the Minister of Finance that there would be an abatement of 15 per cent for the provinces has clarified the situation to some extent. However, the provinces will not necessarily pass on these abatements and are under no obligation to do so. Until a more definite position on the part of the provinces is known, the mining companies will be in some confusion. The proposals in Bill C-259 definitely reduce the incentive to invest money in mining and will relatively reduce the amount of risk capital that will go to the mining industry.
In a recent speech Mr. A. G. Goodeve, president of McIntyre, Porcupine Mines, said:
The most basic uncertainty regarding new provisions relates to exploration, because the investment decisions that must be made now are concerned not with short term but with the eventual rates of return from discoveries not yet made, which must compare favourably with investment opportunities elsewhere.
In revising the tax on the mining industry the government has made the decision that more capital should be directed away from the mining industry and-hopefully- channelled into the manufacturing sector of the economy.
Because of the mining industry's wide dispersion across the country, and its value as often the only industry in large areas of Canada, I think we must look at this tax very closely. Mining is carried on in many of the regions that have been designated under the regional economic expansion program. Under the proposed program, the government is making massive grants to the so-called underdeveloped areas of Canada and grants are being given to many firms that have little hope of becoming viable entities once these grants are discontinued. I think that the restrictions proposed by the federal government just do not make sense. Indeed, the government seems to be reversing its policy in its attempt to rehabilitate these regions by means of grants under the regional economic expansion program. Particularly is this true in western Canada, where mining, oil and gas industries are of extreme value to the economy of the four western provinces. Indeed, in the Yukon these industries are virtually the mainstay of the economy. In Manitoba towns like Thompson, Flin Flon and Lynn Lake are almost wholly dependent in economic terms upon the mining industry. The government has made a calculated effort to discriminate against communities on the periphery of the country in order to build up a central manufacturing industry.
It is generally accepted that there is adequate replacement of minerals from sources in the world other than Canada and at prices that are quite competitive. Cutbacks in the mining industry will only compound the problem of job creation and favourable trade balances that are so necessary for the 1970's. The unsettled international economic and monetary situation holds such serious potential consequences for Canada that we must view this aspect of the bill which relates to mining with some grave misgivings.

A recent report by the Science Council of Canada entitled "Innovation in a Cold Climate" illustrates why it is so dangerous to tamper with the taxation structure for Canadian mining at this time. The mining and petroleum industries are two outstanding Canadian sectors which have shown the capacity over the years to successfully compete in world markets. With regard to manufacturing, pages 20 and 21 of the Council's report read:
Growth, competitive ability, and profits go hand in hand. All three appear to be lacking in the Canadian Manufacturing Industry at the moment.-
Together, however, these trends represent a threat of unusual severity and duration. Additional complications have also begun to appear: the United States import surcharge, the rising exchange rate, and the possible recurrence of inflation, for example.-
__if these trends continue and there are no signs in the last four
years of their improvement or even of their arrest -Canada's economy in this decade will increasingly become dependent on the resource and service industries.
If the council's views are correct, they surely add further support to the contention which the mining industry has repeatedly made; namely that with so many other industries in Canada in difficulty, it makes no sense, especially in these anxious times, to tamper with the taxation structure which has enabled the mining industry to develop successfully and thereby contribute so importantly to the over-all economic growth of this country.
I feel that the government has made major changes in the taxation structure of the mining industry. We do not know where this will lead. All indications are that there will be a dampening of mining activity in view of the heavy increase in the work force that is necessary in Canada and will occur in the 1970's. This indicates that the government has not acted wisely in its handling of the mining industry in Bill C-259.

One proposal which will have the most serious effect on the greatest number of Canadians is that dealing with the change in the method of taxation of co-operatives and credit unions. I know this subject has been brought up many times in this debate. Many speakers on both sides of the House have stood in their place and have affirmed their strong support for the co-operative. Many government members have made these statements. However, I have yet to see any concrete evidence that this government intends to accept any of the suggestions or proposals put forward either from the government side of the House or from our side. I know there is an amendment which I shall not discuss now other than to say it does not satisfy the criticism that these tax changes will be very damaging to the co-operatives. After all, co-operatives are a special type of business. Certainly, they have been treated differently.
The criticism has been made often that co-operatives have received tax advantages at the expense of other businesses. I cannot agree with that statement because the co-operatives are subject to a type of taxation that is unique in this country to co-operatives and is unique in the world. I refer of course to the arbitrary method of taxing on the capital employed concept. This is a discriminatory method of collecting taxes and to the best of my knowledge it is not found in any other tax system in the world. Why should there be a difference? What is the logic of taxing on the capital employed in a business. I have been in business all my life and have never seen such a concept in private business. The amount of capital employed in a business has nothing to do with its income and should not be the basis for levying income tax.
Co-operatives are different from other enterprises primarily because of their objectives. They are self-help organizations. Incidentally, with all the criticism in respect of United States ownership I would point out that co-operatives are always Canadian and locally owned. These self-help organizations are generally found in primary production areas, namely, grain, dairying, farm products and fishing. The merchandising they carry on actually is a service to the people in the small centres which in many cases is not supplied by private enterprise because it is not profitable. The question I should like to ask is, should city people be denied the right to self-help organization recognition because their attempts to cut living costs cause some profit oriented corporations to lose some business? Co-operatives usually serve members

I also submit that co-operatives are partnerships in selfhelp efforts and the members are bound together by a common cause that is comparable to that of any of the partnerships I have named. Cannot farmers combine to form a partnership to sell their grain? Does it matter if there are 10 farmers or 10,000? Is not the principle the same? I submit that co-operatives compete with individual entrepreneurs, partnerships as well as corporations. Their objectives in forming a co-operative are practically the same as the partnership which I described, that is self-help. The patronage returns method of disposing of earnings, if unrestricted by capital employed capital tax, results in taxation at individual level of owners of partnership co-operatives. This was the method of taxation recommended in the Carter report. Therefore, I submit that it is equitable and reasonable that the income of co-operatives allocated to members be taxed at individual levels and reserves retained be taxed at appropriate corporate rates.
I admit that there is nothing new in these proposals, but I am trying to throw a little new light on the matter and to point out to the officials as well as to the minister that co-operatives are basically partnerships. Many types of partnerships exist in business. Why are the co-operatives singled out for special discriminatory tax on the capital employed basis? If the minister or his officials can satisfy me or can point out to me any similar cases of partnerships being taxed in this way, then possibly I would be able to accept their arguments. However, until such time as they can give us on this side of the House a satisfactory explanation why co-operatives are being singled out for discriminatory treatment, we will continue to fight these clauses when they come before the committee. We will continue to hope that somehow or other we can persuade this government that co-operatives in this country render too vital a service to be taxed out of existence.
Income Tax Act

I rise to take part in this debate on Bill C-259, an act to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to the act. If this bill does nothing else, it will provide an opportunity to debate the government's economic failures, and for that we must be grateful. However, the country is not grateful for the mess in which the government has left the nation's finances. On all sides we see the total failure of anti-poverty programs which never got off the paper on which they were written, the increasing menace of unemployment, the fear and uncertainty of industry and the worsening climate of confidence. That is the government's record, a record of failure and fear.
Hear, hear!

The bill before the House represents the obituary of the hopes with which this government came to power less than four years ago. The amendments which our party put forward, and which were defeated, highlighted the government's failure in the economic field, the unacceptable level of unemployment, inflation, the crisis condition of industry, the lack of confidence in the government, and the fact that the proposed bill does nothing to remedy these serious conditions. The bill is a shadow and a fraud. It contains 700 pages of imcomprehensible amendments to an act that has already been subjected to repeated amendments over the years. You call that reform, but it is only piling confusion on top of confusion and confounding even the lawyers of this country who frankly confess that the entire tax law, with the addition of the present bill, is not only meaningless but impossible to understand.
I refer in passing to the arrival in this country of a young Russian seaman who jumped from a ship, swam for two hours through the icy coastal waters of British Columbia, and climbed a high cliff just to be in Canada. If he had seen this legislation, he would have turned around and swum back. I hope that the government will allow this young man to stay in Canada. Anything else would be unthinkable. This is the kind of immigrant we need in this country.
One that can swim.

A week or two ago, the income figures were released and they showed which cities in Canada had the highest income level. It will be interesting for my Waffle friends in the NDP to note that Oakville, where there is a Ford automobile plant led all the rest, including Toronto and Edmonton. I wonder what the NDP solution would be once they got rid of all the U.S. industry? Would they put everyone on the federal government payroll? There would be total regimentation.
The present legislation is a fraud because in reality it does not represent tax reform. What it represents is an attempt by the government to carry out the principle of taxing Canadians to the fullest extent that the traffic will bear. The government has been spending money like a drunken sailor. They are running huge deficits and are now at the point, as we have seen recently, where they no longer pay the Wheat Board what belongs to the Wheat Board by statute. Maybe they cannot afford to keep up the payments to the Wheat Board. But apparently they are

able to find $15 million for an experiment to see whether people will lose the incentive to work if they are placed on welfare. Do we need any further experiments in that direction? I can assure the government that if they want to supply me with the necessary income to maintain a standard of living to which I would like to become accustomed, something on a par with the Prime Minister, for example, then I will guarantee to lose the incentive to work. There was $15 million for experiments in sociology, but nothing for the western farmer. There was $40 million for the Opportunities for Youth program, but nothing for the poor and aged.
The government can always find unlimited funds for the kookie ideas but no money to take care of the essential business. This is a government which goes out and buys a new hat when there is no food on the table. I hope the Prime Minister does better on his housekeeping accounts than he has been doing at balancing the nation's business. We have asked for tax cuts, industry has asked for tax cuts, the poor bloody taxpayers always ask for tax cuts. The only thing the government is cutting is the taxpayer's windpipe. Tax cuts would increase consumer demand, stimulate industry, increase employment and put Canada back in competition. The government will not listen because they are obsessed with the old Liberal philosophy of tax and tax, spend and spend, and waste and waste. They call that redistribution. The Minister of Finance regards himself as a kind of pipe-smoking Robin Hood, taking from the poor to give to the rich. The only problem is that he does not have Friar Tuck and Little John to guide him.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: How about the man from Georgia?

The present bill is a gigantic monument to the government's inability to come to terms with reality. It represents the final stage of a long process which began under the Diefenbaker government with the setting up of the Carter Royal Commission on taxation. That commission brought forward a number of new principles, most of which have been thrown by the wayside in this legislation. The Carter Commission inaugurated the policy of taxation based on equity. There is no shadow of equity anywhere in these amendments.
Then, we had the white paper on taxation. Perhaps the present bill could be called the black paper. The white paper made the House and the country aware of the theorizing and speculative conjectures of the minister and his officials. It was a kind of almanac of taxation possibilities, none of which were ever realized. Then came the present legislation, if I can use that term in relation to the hodge-podge before us, which betrayed and discarded both the white paper and the Carter Commission. In the bill before the House there is no trace of Carter and very little of the white paper. What we have here is a vise to squeeze the taxpayer, the farmer, the householder, business and industry.
This legislation will have an inflationary impact such as we have not yet seen in this country. It will push up prices, stifle industry, and reduce the standard of living of 30 per cent of the people of this country. The reason it is needed is that the government has wasted so much that it must

now extract every last cent from the taxpayer. The bill is the government's attempt to prove that you can squeeze blood from a stone if you squeeze hard enough.
This bill should not be allowed to pass because it is a bad bill. It introduces a new principle in Canadian politics, the principle of legal confiscation. Everyone can understand taxing a dollar. But when the same dollar is taxed over and over, that is no longer taxation, that is confiscation. A dollar is taxed when an individual receives it as income. It is further taxed as a return on investment. It is taxed once again as profit. It is taxed when he dies, and passes it on to his heirs. We used to complain about double taxation. This bill brings in triple and quadruple taxation, and gives the government the right to go as far as it likes.
This legislation carries on a process which has been growing more and more destructive, taking capital out of productive purposes and diverting it to non-productive experimentation. When money is spent on social theorizing there is no return on the investment. It is removed from the economy. That means that people who are interested in producing and contributing have to work harder to find more money elsewhere in order to produce, to build, to create, to explore and develop. The government is not concerned about these things, but non-productive distribution has resulted in slowing down the wheels of industry, putting a stop to development, and giving us the highest unemployment in history.
So far, we have been able to get by on our resources. As the hon. member for Duvernay pointed out the other day-and he is one of the greatest philosophers in the Liberal hierarchy-living on our resources is like living on capital. We all know how far that goes. I want to commend his speech on the economic situation, and his grasp of the essentials of Canada's position when we are being asked by the government to surrender our heritage for a mess of American pottage.
The hon. member for Duvernay, who should have been the Minister of Finance, gave a realistic appraisal of the present situation, one the government could study with profit. The present illogical and theoretical approach cannot go on without destroying the economy entirely. What level of unemployment, what level of inflation is the government prepared to tolerate before it will act? How long is it going to try to deal with problems through seminars, task forces and position papers? Canadians are suffering all across this land, and the government is playing tiddleywinks with taxation reform that is not reform but simply a tightening of the screw on the taxpayer.
The hon. member for Duvernay said, "Cut taxes on lower income and middle income groups." Instead of that the government is raising them. Is it not curious indeed that some of the brighter minds in the Liberal hierarchy have had enough of this shilly-shallying and tinkering? The hon. member for Duvernay is one. The former minister of defence, the hon. member for Trinity, is one. The former member for York West has parted company with the little group at the top, presumably because there was no room at the top. They are all honourable and honest men who decided that the fate of Canada concerned them more than the fate of the government. That is what we are asking the government to do. Think about Canada, about the unemployed, about inflation, about the western

farmer, about the housewife who, as a result of this legislation if it passes, will have to pay even more than she now does to put food on the table and educate her children.
The government is taking more and more from the private sector and frittering it away in a series of socialist experiments. Money frittered away by the government does not produce economic activity, does not produce jobs, does not help production and development. It keeps a lot of people working in the high echelons of government think-tanks, but that does not help unemployment. This legislation should not be allowed to pass this House for the simple reason that it does not approach the problem of tax reform on a basis of equity or economic development. It is just another move in imposing on the Canadian people a new set of theories emanating from the government.
When you consistently avoid the problems and deal with those things which exist only in your own mind, then you are creating serious and long-lasting trouble in the economy. That is what the government is doing. It is simply tilting at strawmen while Canadians are suffering. The economy is running downhill because of indifference and neglect. There is no reason for this policy except ineptness and stupidity on the part of the government. A little incentive, and a little leadership in the form of widespread tax cuts might mean cutting back on some of the programs which the government's advisers love to dream up. At the same time, it would mean that many more Canadians would be working, many more Canadians would be eating better, dressing better, and paying less, and we would be in a position to take up the slack in the economy caused by the Nixon measures.
I just want to make one point on the Nixon measures. Personally, I have respect for President Nixon's integrity and his qualities as a human being. There is no doubt he is growing into his job. But I cannot accept the fact that Canada should be penalized for the Americans' failure to stay competitive. Nor can I, along with many other Canadians, accept the sheep-like attitude of the present government. The Minister of Finance went to Washington and, while he was blowing smoke in their eyes, they pulled the wool over his. Is it not time the government stood up and told Washington that we are their best customer? I am not advocating a trade war with the United States. That would be suicide. I am advocating that the government take a firm position for once-

Mr. Chairman, before I resume the debate, I should like to call your attention to something. I do not want, Mr. Chairman, to bring this point up as a question of privilege. There has been some attempt lately to lower the corporate tax by 7 per cent and personal income tax by 3 per cent, but what is the minister trying to do? As I said earlier, our unemployment figures are the highest in the world. This has forced, and I emphasize that word, the Minister of Finance to revise his policies and bring in yet a third budget this session. I do not know Canadian history all that well, but I think that three budgets in one

session is a precedent. However, I commend the minister for trying to do his best.
I observe you are getting restless, Mr. Chairman, so I will finish on this note. I find it very hard to equate this 7 per cent and 3 per cent tax reduction with jobs, especially in view of the way the minister seeks to implement those cuts. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on the oil and gas industry as it relates to Bill C-259. The most important feature of oil and gas exploration is the cash flow of money in order to control land for exploration and development. After 25 years of extremely active exploration and development in western Canada, the hunt for oil is spreading to the far north, offshore areas and Hudson Bay. What concerns the oil and gas industry most is the attitude of governments to the extractive industries, particularly as exemplified in Bill C-259.
Mr. W. O. Twaits of Imperial Oil forecast a sum of $25 billion will be required for the Canadian petroleum industry over the next ten years. Others have suggested that this may be too high by $10 billion, but in any case the figure is enormous. What is the basic source of funds for this industry? In the statistics comparing the operations of a group of companies in the years 1960 to 1969 that control just under 50 per cent of all oil and gas production and 90 per cent of all refining and sales capacity, it was revealed that in 1960 usage of funds for capital stock was
31.5	per cent of the total; retained earnings amounted to
30.5	per cent for a total equity base of 62 per cent; short term debt was 22.1 per cent; and long term debt was 15.9 per cent. In 1969 capital stock had gone down to 22 per cent, retained earnings had risen to 36 per cent. In other words, capital stock declined by 25 per cent while retained earnings went up by 20 per cent.
This really means a greatly reduced injection of private capital into the equity base of the Canadian petroleum industry during the past ten years. Long term debt increased by one-third, which means that the large companies were able to procure more capital than smaller companies.
There are three basic sources of capital for this industry. First of all, there is the self-generated cash flow. Second, there is public participation, which can be had on an equity base for common or preferred shares and sold to the public, to pension funds, mutual funds, life insurance and trust funds within the limitation of govenment statutes. All the funds I have mentioned so far must come from the private investor, either from his savings or from his earnings on his savings. In recent years, the issuing of debentures has generally involved a substantially increased return to the lender. The third source of funds is money provided through government sources, such as by the Canada Development Corporation, though it seems doubtful that this source would be very profitable.
All of this adds up to a tremendous demand for capital in Canada by this industry over the next decade. However, all levels of government as well as industry are being asked to look for their investment money to the domestic

market. In 1969 the oil industry generated 36 per cent of its needs internally, the other 63 per cent having to come from sources outside the industry. The Canadian public contributed less than 5 per cent of this capital need on an equity basis. The oil and gas industry in the eight years between 1962 and 1969 earned 8 per cent on invested capital, compared with other industries such as mining which earned 10 per cent. Not many industries were this low. Where is the oil and gas industry getting its funds today? More and more it is going to United States sources, tapping individuals and offering participatory units or drilling units for as little as $5,000. These investments can enter this country on a preferential after-tax basis in competition with Canadian money.
What does Bill C-259 provide to remedy this situation? A United States taxpayer can reduce his income by the amount of the loss if his oil well drilling turned out to be a "bust". As far as the Canadian taxpayer is concerned, for a long time no such relief was offered him. In this bill the government is providing for only a 20 per cent write-off per year. I am not sure whether this write-off is on a diminishing basis or on a straight-line basis, as suggested in the white paper, and I hope the Minister of Finance will enlighten me in this regard. If it is on a diminishing basis, it will take about 26 years before it is completely written off, and I therefore suggest this is no way to offer incentives to Canadians to buy into their own oil and gas industry. If we want our Canadian citizens to be involved in the oil and gas industry, we will have to do something with this. It will be much better to have Canadians buy into their own oil and gas industry rather than to have the government attempt to use vast sums of the taxpayers' money through the Canada Development Corporation to give Canadians control of this industry.
I now turn to the depletion allowance. The Independent Petroleum Association appeared before the other place yesterday. It feels that the abatement of the depletion concept, as it is generally understood in the world-wide oil industry, and its replacement with the concept of earned depletion will not generate the necessary capital for the Canadian petroleum industry. We believe that taxpayers with oil and gas income should be entitled to gross depletion. If the government does not accept our recommendation of the gross depletion concept, then we consider that the earned depletion as proposed in the legislation would be more meaningful.
Failing an acceptance of the gross depreciation concept, the Independent Petroleum Association suggests that all Canadian exploration and development expenses, as defined in clause 66 (15) (b), should be included in determining the earned depletion base, but to avoid any abuse in the sale of properties between companies, it is suggested that income from such sales should be credited to Canadian companies' development and exploration expenses and thus the total earned depletion base does not change. The new changes have caused considerable unease and lack of direction about how they will be effective. It is hoped they will not be as bad as some feel. Apparently the government is departing from the present concept of depletion into an unknown field, a field in which other countries have very little experience.

I now turn to the Canadian pulp and paper industry. I wish to say a few words about this industry because it is one of our large employers, but it seems to have deteriorated in the last decade. At this time there are numerous announcements of lay-offs which indicate that the pulp and paper industry is in some difficulty. A brief was prepared by the Canadian pulp and paper industry and submitted to the Minister of Finance in October, 1970. It contained a general set of proposals. The pulp and paper industry seems to have made a case for a study of a new basis of taxation for that industry. Since the pulp and paper industry is dealing with a renewable resource, it cannot advance the same argument as the mining, oil and gas industries which deal with a nonrenewable resource. Therefore, we have to make a decision as to whether or not we can accept their argument.
If the Canadian pulp and paper industry can maintain a growth rate of 6 per cent a year, which is approximately the world growth rate, it will mean about one million tons of pulp. This would provide an estimated 5,000 jobs in the mills and woodlands with considerable multiplier effects. Although Canadian production of pulp and paper has increased in recent years, the industry has lost its position in a number of its markets. Canada's share of the United States newsprint market dropped from 77 per cent in 1955 to 64 per cent in 1970. In 1955, Canada produced 54 per cent of the free world supply of newsprint. In 1970, the share was down to 41 per cent. There has been a corresponding decline in all the statistics relevant to world trade in pulp and paper. The main competitors of the Canadian pulp and paper industry are located in the United States and Scandinavia. Canada has vast forest resources with a skilled labour force, but this is offset by higher transportation costs, machinery costs, corporation taxes and other factors.
In a brief presented to the federal government in 1971, the pulp and paper industry stated that corporation taxes in Canada are considerably higher than those applying to their counterparts in the United States and Sweden. In the United States, the value of timber may be classed as a capital gain and taxed at a lower rate. A compilation of the corporate tax rate in Canada and the United States shows rates in the United States to be from 43 to 49 per cent of income while in Canada rates vary from 51 to 54 per cent. More important, the weighted average of taxes paid as a percentage of income, comparing United States companies with Canadian companies, shows the average rate of the United States company to be 34 per cent while that of the Canadian company is 49 per cent.
Corporations in Sweden have tax advantages resulting from liberal depreciation allowances, a lower over-all rate of taxation, the use of value-added taxes in place of sales taxes and the provision of tax-free investment reserves. It is estimated that the corporation tax rate in Sweden is 40 per cent as compared to 51 to 54 per cent in Canada. I wish to quote from The Tax System in Sweden published by Stockholm's Enskilda Bank, November, 1969:
Swedish tax rules "have contributed to the efficiency 6f Swedish industry as a competitor in world markets ... These Swedish tax devices constitute an arsenal of tax weapons, probably unmatched elsewhere in the world, which may serve as a fertile source of ideas for the business man, government official, tax practioneer, or economist seeking ways to use taxation to strengthen corporate liquidity and offset business cycle fluctuations."

In Finland, the 31 per cent devaluation of the Finmark in 1967, and the related fiscal policies, placed the industry in that country in a particularly advantageous position to improve its place as a world supplier of forest products. The sharp increase in capacity in the period 1970-71 has resulted from government policies fostering the export industries. The Canadian pulp and paper industry has made its case that it needs incentives and a revamping of the tax structure. It is well known that the pulp and paper industry is not as profitable as it has been in the past. An account in a Montreal newspaper approximately one month ago indicated that many plants in Quebec were approaching obsolescence and that very few new ones had been built.
Bill C-259 does not seem to provide any improvements in the tax structure, although dropping the corporation tax by 7 per cent as announced last Thursday will be helpful, but this provision will expire at the end of 1972. It seems unlikely that the industry will respond without future encouragement. The pulp and paper industry is dealing with a renewable resource. It provides jobs in many so-called underdeveloped areas that are receiving grants under the regional economic expansion program. In many cases the government would be well advised to consider the tax structure of industries indigent to the area rather than the elaborate subventions granted by members of the civil service. I feel that Bill C-259 has created uncertainty in the mining, oil and gas industry. It does not seem to have much to offer for the pulp and paper industry in the future, either.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak again on Bill C-259,1 want to continue with the general theme that I find the government in error. I refer to the failure of the government to reinstate confidence^ in the business community. It will be very difficult for the 7 per cent reduction in corporates taxes announced by the minister in his budgetary statement of a week ago to really have the beneficial effect the government expected it to have and which I believe all Canadians wish it would have in creating more employment. Bill C-259 brings about changes in the corporate tax structure and many significant changes in what one might call foreign investment within Canada. I think now it has become pretty clear that a great deal of our economic policy will hinge upon our foreign policy. It once was said by a number of people that a country's defence policy should be in tune with its foreign policy. I think it is now true that the government is attempting to tie its corporate policy to its foreign policy. In order to instil confidence within the nation and within the business community we must take a look at our foreign policy. I do not intend to do that at this time, but I think one really has to draw that parallel. Surely, we are divorcing ourselves from the economic atmosphere and environment of the United States through a number of measures.
Bill C-259 deals with foreign investment in two or three subtle ways and perhaps, as the editorial in the Toronto Star of October 20 suggests, Canada should emphasize that 50 per cent or 51 per cent of a corporation should be owned by Canadians and, second, that all new foreign investment that is proposed should be screened by a government board or body. Actually, this will happen under

October 22, 1971
Income Tax Act
Bill C-256 when it passes, at least the competitive aspect. Then again, the question of foreign investment and the size of corporations that will be allowed to sell out to United States or foreign concerns is dealt with very fully in this particular piece of legislation. They will have to pay the difference between the 50 per cent rate of taxation and the 25 per cent rate of taxation.
This lack of confidence in the business community, of course, is compounded by the difficulty arising out of the United States surtax and the attitude of that country. It is now commonly believed by many Canadians that the United States government is not going to be overly anxious to please Canada by removing the surtax or to give Canada the special status we have enjoyed in the past because of our continental position with the United States. The United States is not prepared to do this now, at least partly because of our foreign policy, our policy of supporting the Albanian resolution at the United Nations. Let us accept the situation as it is. Perhaps we are now shifting toward the Russian economic sphere. One might wonder where that will lead us and whether or not we are encouraging Russian investment within our corporate structure and whether this will bring about renewed confidence within the Canadian economy. I might refer to Time magazine of March 29 which deals at length with the Russian economy and states:
For the first time in history, the new Soviet five-year plan, which will be approved at the present Congress, assigns a fractionally higher growth rate to the consumer-oriented industries .. .
I think this is very important because it has been said often we do not want to appear to be solely drawers of water and hewers of wood in respect of the United States but want to become an industrial economy. In some parts of Canada we are well on the way to becoming an industrial country and want to continue this. If we are to shift our trade to Russia, then we want to become an industrial country and not merely be hewers of wood and carriers of water for Russia.
It is helpful to note that Russia is shifting its position to a higher growth rate in consumer oriented industries than in respect of the "metal eaters" of heavy industry. Even so, the metal eaters will continue to receive the great bulk of Soviet industrial investment, the article states. Then further the article suggests that under the present leadership the Russian economy has done fairly well but not well enough. In fact Soviet agriculture, which employs about 26 per cent of the work force versus less than 2 per cent in the United States, has picked up considerably and the Soviets have not had to buy wheat abroad for two years. However, there are still shortages of meat, fruit and fresh vegetables. Industry is lagging badly. Technological advance is falling even farther behind that of the west. The consumer remains ill cared for. So perhaps we have a role as an industrial country in trading with the U.S.S.R. if we would be permitted through some system to supply our industrial goods to that country. Perhaps this would bring about some renewed confidence in Canada.
But what would all this do in respect to our trading partner to the south, the United States. It is interesting to note that even if they should remove the surcharge and other retaliatory acts, we are to some extent quite vulnerable. I should like to quote from the Toronto Telegram of September 7,1971:

Total Canadian investment in the U.S.-direct and portfolio-is $11,773 million while American investment in Canada totals $34,323 million.
Perhaps equally significant from the Canadian viewpoint is the fact that a much greater proportion of U.S. investment is direct-in 'productive facilities' including plants and factories and such fields as petroleum and natural gas and others . . .
As the hon. member for Dauphin pointed out in his speech a few minutes ago more of that investment is entering what is commonly referred to as the extractive industry, resources. The article continues:
Many Canadian ventures are formidable. Carling Brewing Co., a subsidiary of Canadian Breweries, the world's largest beer producer, has seven plants in the U.S. with sales of more than $200 million, greater than those of the Canadian parent.
Massey-Ferguson Ltd., world's largest producer of farm machinery, has eight plants employing 10,000 Americans. The American subsidiary of Distillers Corp.-Seagrams Ltd. controls more than one-fifth of the U.S. liquor market. Hiram Walker and Sons Inc., another Canadian-owned subsidiary, has vast plant and bottling facilities scattered throughout the U.S.
It goes on to suggest that Garfield Weston, the food, bakery and groceteria tycoon, has major outlets in the United States as has the Thomson chain of newspapers which owns 44 dailies and 12 weekly newspapers in the United States. It suggests that much of the present Canadian corporate structure of which Canadians hold majority Canadian ownership also has a dual role in the United States economy so we must be very careful that we do not bring about retaliatory action after the surtax is lifted in order to restore the confidence in the business community within Canada. The attitude that Canada is taking toward the United States at present, which is one of preference for a closer trade and economic alignment with the United States, may well turn out to be very costly to the industrial growth of Canada because much of the industrial investment in Canada is also invested in the U.S.
One interesting point which I think has not been made in this debate, and perhaps should be made, is that much of this loss of confidence stems from the feeling that the United States believed they were getting the short end of the stick in the auto pact and that some changes should be made in order to bring about a greater degree of fairness between the two countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Explain.

Yes, I will explain. Canada said that the auto pact is not negotiable, that we are going to carry on and that we will pay no attention to the wishes of the United States in that regard. This did not bring about any degree of confidence in the business community in Canada. Does the minister wish to ask me a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I was wondering who said that because I certainly did not.
I did not hear the minister's remark, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Does the minister wish to ask a question?
October 22, 1971

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: This is a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I asked who had said that because it certainly cannot be attributed to me. As a matter of fact, our negotiations with the United States on the automobile agreement had been going on for quite a while before we suffered the interruption of the U.S. surcharge.

I appreciate the minister's interruption because I do not want to misinterpret his remarks. If the auto pact is negotiable, that is a very good thing for Canadian industry because it may instil confidence in the industry and it may prevent any retaliatory action by the U.S. Let us assume, however, that we have to adjust our automobile production. I think the auto pact has built up in Canada a tremendous capacity to produce trucks and automobiles. Let us take a look at the Toronto Telegram issue of April 25, 1967, which says the following about the automobile industry:
The capacity of the auto industry has been substantially expanded in order to meet the growing demands of the Canadian market plus the new requirements for the U.S. market. At Ford of Canada, for example, we added a new $25 million truck plant which now operates on a two shift basis- We carried out a $14 million expansion of our Oakville passenger plant- A new passenger plant has been constructed at St. Thomas at a cost of $65 million.
The article goes on to speak about the number of people employed. The point I want to make here is that now that we have built up this capacity it would be shameful if, through some negotiations with the U.S., we failed to employ the capitalization that has been poured into that industrial complex.
I notice in today's Gazette an article which says that after Mr. Kosygin's visit to Canada the Soviets will want a super deal for wheat and prefabs. The Prime Minister said today during the question period that no new wheat sales would be forthcoming and the communique did not deal with wheat. The Soviets-are going to take the three and a half million tons under the present contract, which would take up until April of next year, but they are interested in prefabs. If we are attempting to divorce ourselves from the U.S. economic sphere, perhaps we should look for some way in which to use the capitalization in the auto industry.
I have here a book called "Soviet Transport Experience" which describes the recent troubles in the U.S.S.R. in transportation. The book was published as late as 1969 and it suggests that the production of trucks in the U.S.S.R. is not keeping up with the demand in that country. At page 177 of the book we find the following statement:
Recent scrappage rates in Soviet agriculture imply that a truck would be on hand for 30 years, not necessarily always in operable condition.
The book gives statistics regarding the number of trucks produced and it suggests that, with the growth in transportation and the increased number of roads built, hard surfaced and unsurfaced, what might be called a switch from railways to truck transportation is taking place in that country. The book goes on to suggest that the production of trucks in the U.S.S.R. is not keeping up with the demand. After studying that book, perhaps we should consider whether we in Canada, with our expanded truck industry, could make a major breakthrough in the sale of
Income Tax Act
trucks to Russia. This is no particular secret. I remember some time ago when Ford went over to study a truck production plant in the U.S.S.R. but because of U.S. regulations he was prohibited from building a truck plant in that country. Perhaps negotiations could be carried out with the U.S., which wants us to bring about greater fairness toward their country with regard to automotive production, to find out whether they would permit part of Canada's production to be directed to the U.S.S.R.
The book which I mentioned which deals with the Russian transportation experience deals also with the growth and the potential growth in passenger cars. It seems to me that it is difficult to compare roads for passenger travel in Russia with those on the North American continent because, even taking into account their increased road construction, they are far behind this continent. There is a section in the book dealing with growth in passenger travel in the U.S.S.R. Here also agreements could be worked out between our two countries which would allow Canada to sell a limited number of cars which would be produced in our expanded auto production complex.
I throw out these thoughts in the hope that the minister will consider them and see what could be done because my aim is to restore confidence in the business community in Canada so that Canadians will no longer remain on the unemployment list in such large numbers and so that the business community will readily re-invest the 7 per cent which the Minister of Finance suggests in his budgetary statement he is giving back to them. Thus, confidence will be renewed within our industrial complex and Canadians can once again be gainfully employed.
All economic indicators point toward a very dismal winter, but if we are going to switch our production and our economy from the U.S. to Russia, I think we should perhaps explore this automotive concept very closely because automobiles is one of the commodities, in addition to wheat, which perhaps could be sold to the U.S.S.R. I do not want us ending up as hewers of wood and drawers of water for Russia, any more than I want us being that for the United States.

Mr. Chairman, in taking a general, over-all view of the tax bill we have to assess what it will do in terms of improving the position of Canadians. When we look at those portions of the bill dealing with personal taxation I think we must all agree that there are some good points. We can disagree on whether the government has gone far enough or has gone too far in increasing exemptions, but nevertheless the exemptions are welcome. Expenses for child care will now be taken into consideration, and there will be an exemption of up to $150 to workers, mechanics and the like who have to purchase their own tools. All this is a step in the right direction and we are happy that the government finally has acted upon the suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition. Certainly his constructive suggestions have been most helpful to the Minister of Finance when deciding these matters.
The main problems in Canada today are unemployment, an uncertain business climate and lack of the faith in the economy by the manufacturing, agricultural and resource industries. The increased exemptions in the per-

October 22, 1971
Income Tax Act
sonal tax area may mean an extra $50 or $60 a year for a family, but in terms of creating real employment what will the tax bill do? Will it help the resource industries? Will it help the mining and petroleum industries? Will they be able to expand?
The waste paper industry; that is all it helps.

It doesn't do much for the paper industry. Let us see what the Canadian Manufacturers Association has to say with regard to improving the tax bill as it applies to resource industries. Speaking about depreciation, the association says:
The tax reform bill permits resource industries to deduct $1 of depletion for every $3 of defined expenditures up to a maximum of 33 1/3 per cent of production profits. The association is concerned that, apart from the possibility that the new incentive system may prove seriously ineffective, the definition of eligible expenditures is too narrow.
Then they cite a few items which in their opinion have been unreasonably excluded from the eligible expenditure base. The following is one:
Cost of acquiring Crown mineral rights.
Both parliamentary committees thought that this should be included but the minister chose not to heed them.
All capital costs directly associated with the development of oil or gas for market, including field equipment and gas plants.
Exploration and development costs incurred in the "vicinity" of an existing mine.
These are not included and their exclusion will discourage expansion of our major industries.
What will the bill do for the agricultural industry? It certainly will not do much for farmers. If they have a small personal income it will provide them with an extra $50, $60, or $70 a year. On the other hand, it will bring their recaptured depreciation into income, which will mean that they will be taxed on an extra $3,000 or $4,000. We will give them a little on the one hand, and on the other take away three or four times as much.
The proposed capital gains tax will be difficult to live with, and certainly many people in agriculture will not be able to do much to protect themselves from extra tax in this area. This tax will be mainly applied against the small and middle-income earners, those who cannot protect themselves against it because of the great expense involved in hiring experts to advise them.
The United States has had a capital gains tax in effect for some time. It does not affect the most wealthy people. They have title-holding companies which theoretically, so far as the tax department is concerned, provide them with exemptions. There is nothing in this tax bill that will take care of such a situation. People who are wealthy enough will be able to discover the loopholes and escape the provisions of the legislation. Regarding the provisions with respect to international competitiveness, the Canadian Manufactures Association has this to say:
The proposals with respect to international income are more onerous than those applied elsewhere and would inhibit Canadian companies' efforts to sell and expand abroad. In addition, we think the over-all impact of the bill would add somewhat to a corporation's costs. Recent developments in the United States increase our concern on these two points.

This is a reference to the U.S. surcharge and DISC proposal. In light of new developments with the United States we need to reassess the tax bill and the tax structure as it applies to the international situation.
Every few days in this House the Prime Minister tries to reassure us that business is picking up and that there will be a renewal of confidence. But what are the manufacturers doing, Mr. Chairman? We have one example of our only domestic manufacturer of tractors-the remainder being imported from the United States, Sweden, Russia and Roumania-who is now residing in Mexico and is reported to be contemplating taking out citizenship in that country. We can assume that he is also contemplating moving his headquarters to that country, so his confidence in what the future holds for Canada cannot be very great. If this happens, then of course we will have another foreign-owned company. This indicates what business thinks of the economic climate in Canada.
I suggest that these reassurances given in the House by the Prime Minister are futile and a waste of time, considering the reaction of business leaders and manufacturers. Of late the Prime Minister has been assuming the role of the great internationalist developing relations around the globe. In some ways this is commendable, but I do not think Canadians want to jeopardize their standard of living for the sake of the Prime Minister presenting himself as a great internationalist or mediator.
It must be remembered that about 80 per cent of our manufactured production goes to the United States, especially that of U.S.-controlled firms. We cannot overlook the realities of life. Even those who talk about economic nationalism in this House want a nice comfortable house to go home to; they want to know that the pay cheque is coming at the end of the month and that their standard of living at least remains stable or possibly improves a little. If our relationships with the United States are destroyed, we will suffer.
The hon. member for Crowfoot referred to the role of this country as hewers of wood and drawers of water. What are our chief exports to China and Russia at the present time? Do we export to them the same type of goods that we send to the United States in large quantities? Is it likely, considering their supply of cheap labour, that the Chinese will accept the same quantity of manufactured goods as the United States will? It would be unrealistic to expect this. The imposition of the 10 per cent surcharge on manufactured goods by the United States may give us an opportunity to develop our own manufacturing industry.
I hear a child crying in our public gallery.
He is listening to what I am saying; he is responding.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: It is quiet despair.
Even before he can read this 707-page document, he is crying.

That child will tell his grandchildren not to vote for you.
October 22, 1971
He will tell them he heard.

The majority of Canadians will understand the tax bill just about as well as the child that is crying in the gallery right now. This 707-page is as thick as four Eaton's catalogues. The child's understanding of that document is about as great as that of hon. members on the other side of the House.
And he is crying about it!

Mr. Chairman, we may very well be worse off being regarded as hewers of wood and drawers of water if we do not heed the cries of necessity from below the border and continue to imperil our relations with the United States. The Prime Minister is often asked what he is doing to improve this relationship, but he does not have very much to say about it. During the past six months he should have visited Washington in an effort to reach greater understanding. Instead, he goes skiing or takes trips to countries that are interested only in our great natural resources. It is this indifference to the realities of international diplomacy and the real needs of the Canadian people that has put us in the catastrophic position in which we find ourselves today.

Mr. Chairman, Bill C-259 which was introduced last June under very different circumstances from those we face today, has taken up some time of the House. I have not participated in the debate so far and I hope I will not intrude too long on the committee's time this afternoon.
I suggest, for the sake of argument, that even if this bill was a masterpiece at the time it was introduced-and I doubt that; I do not believe it a-it is not what we require for our country at this stage of its progress, particularly in view of the United States policy introduced on August 15. I would like to use the analogy of a wartime aircraft. We might develop an aircraft which would have been suitable for the last war but which will not be good enough for any war of the future. This bill is like that: the whole picture has changed.
I think the government's policy in preparing Bill C-259 was designed to some extent to discourage the flow of foreign capital to Canada and to increase the investment in Canadian industries by Canadians. Although that aim is laudable, I do not believe the legislation goes far enough in that regard. I do not believe that this income tax revision will in the end result in Canadians being on an even footing with foreigners so far as investing in the resources of this country is concerned. However, at least a small, faltering step has been taken. Under the present situation our capital requirements are substantially different. Actually, I suggest that we depend more than ever on foreign capital and that there is a greater need for it now than there was prior to August 15.
The new economic policies adopted by the United States have resulted in encouraging a retrenchment of their foreign operations. Whereas the United States might have encouraged its corporations and other enterprises to invest in businesses or other undertakings in Canada, West Germany and elsewhere, before the new policies were announced, the interest of the United States is now
Income Tax Act
focused in centres such as Pittsburgh and Cleveland. There will be an increase in the rate of the withdrawal of capital from Canada, or at least there will be a marked slowdown at the rate in which capital comes into this country. Although it may not be so apparent to the people of Ontario, people living in the part of the country I have the honour to represent, or in the province of Quebec across the river, realize that capital is required to create opportunities for Canadians so that they may make the best of their lives as well as strengthen the country in the long run.
I believe it is a matter of record, Mr. Chairman, that Canadians make substantial capital investment. I believe the figures indicate that on a per capita basis Canadians invest more in the United States than the people of the United States invest in Canada. On a per capita basis we invest three times as much. In my view, proper tax legislation at this time ought to be aimed at encouraging the return of that Canadian capital for use in this country. Yet we find that the tax systems of other countries are such that Canadians prefer to invest in those countries rather than in the enterprises in this country.
I suggest that the new economic policies of the United States have been caused by the current economic crisis, the greatest since the depression of the 1930s. Here, again, I should like to use an analogy to illustrate my meaning. During the late 1930s the government of Canada established a royal commission to study dominion-provincial relations. It was known as the Rowell-Sirois commission. That commission did its work late in the 1930s and issued its report, I believe, in 1940. Of course, since the commission had done most of its work during peacetime, when its report came out did not reflect the situation then existing. It was realized, therefore, when the commission reported that the government could not adopt its recommendations because circumstances had changed so greatly. The country was then involved in the war effort, and common sense prevailed.
I do not know what name one could give to our present situation. I think we are witnessing a love affair with systems analyses, or something of that kind. This government seems to feel that everything must happen by a certain time, and that if something does not happen by a certain time it should not happen at all. There seems to be undue concern about January 1, 1972. The government's attitude leads me to conclude that by January 1, 1972, we shall be pretty close to "1984".
The government wanted to produce a grain stabilization program for this country. Because the bill did not proceed in the manner the government thought it ought to proceed, the bill was withdrawn. That is to say, because the government could not get it through in the time allotted, it decided not to go ahead with it at all. The same suggestions are being made with regard to this legislation. We are told that consideration must be finished before January 1, 1972. On the other hand, this tax legislation, in my view, is obsolete and should not be proceeded with.
Our taxation system is not that bad. I think if we look at it on an international basis we will find that Canada is considered as having a relatively good tax system. Yet we are not satisfied with it. We are to do away with the system we have and replace it with a system nobody understands. I suppose it is too much to hope that the

October 22, 1971
Income Tax Act
government will postpone the operation of this law for one year. If that cannot be done, there should be an undertaking by the government that it will not proclaim the great bulk of the bill until the taxpayers and provinces who will be greatly affected by it understand the legislation. We must understand it before it is fully implemented.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If our taxation system is so good, why did the right hon. member for Prince Albert ask Carter to look into it?

That is something I have wondered about. I do not think he asked Mr. Carter to produce a brand new system. I think he asked Carter to simplify the existing system. Surely the name of Carter must conjure up nightmares for the right hon. member for Prince Albert, because Carter did not follow the instructions that were given to him. I do not think this country owes a debt of any nature to the late Kenneth Carter, because he did not do what he was supposed to do.
Is the hon. member talking about instructions Carter was given in private or in writing?
Who said anything about private instructions?
Who is speaking from behind the curtains?
Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River wishes to say something, perhaps he would say it from his seat.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River may ask the question only if the hon. member for Palliser agrees.
Agreed, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the hon. member if it is not true that the terms of reference relating to the Carter report asked Mr. Carter and his colleagues to look into all aspects of our tax system and did not preclude the possibility of bringing in a new system.
He was not asked to write a socialist bible.

As my hon. friend from Calgary North suggests, he was not asked to write a socialist bible. He was asked to look into all aspects of the existing tax system with a view to simplyfing it, not to making it more complicated.
Why bother, if it was such a perfect tax law?

I did not say it was a perfect tax law. I said it was generally recognized in the international community as being a good tax law. The effects of these proposals are unknown to the ordinary taxpayer. Moreover, they are unknown to the provinces. The Minister of Finance tells us there is to be a guarantee that provincial income will be maintained, but no one can understand the

formula which he has proposed to make good this assurance. Gift tax and estate tax are to be dropped and replaced by a capital gains tax, but the federal government has given no undertaking to share the proceeds of that tax with the provinces in the way in which the gift tax and estate tax were formerly shared.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: We give them all.
I beg you pardon.
He does not know.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: It is not hard to know as much as the hon. member for Calgary North.

The government's attitude is that once it has received a mandate from the people it can do anything it pleases until the next election. If the people do not like it, then in the phrase of the Prime Minister they can lump it. In my view that is not a proper way in which to manage this country. The government is forcing the taxpayers to acquiesce in its aims and this places a very high responsibility upon the government for the damage which is likely to result from the legislation before us.
The government is forcing most provinces-all of them, I suppose, with the exception of Quebec which has its own tax machinery-to accept this system. The provinces have no choice, because they lack the facilities to collect taxes on their own behalf. The Minister of Finance says to the provinces, "If you do not like the deal we are offering, then raise your own taxes." But the facilities do not exist. The government is making use of this situation in order to coerce the provinces into agreeing to its proposals. I do not think it can be denied that this measure will have the effect of raising more money for the treasury. The tax base is substantially broadened. It is just a question of making collection by the federal government easier.
I should like to say a word about the mines and minerals provision in the bill. My hon. friend from Battle River has already referred to it and I believe my hon. friend from Dauphin has also done so. I should like to lend my support to their pleas for amendments to the legislation with respect to depletion allowances. I feel the provisions in the bill as it stands are not adequate. Reference has been made to the cost of acquiring land, to the restriction on depletion allowances in that connection. There is also the question of the further facilities which are required in order to carry on an efficient operation once the company has been established.
These mines are often situated in remote areas and developers are required to build houses, construct streets, put in power lines and all the other utilities which go to making up a viable community. I know that at the present time in Alberta the MacIntyre Porcupine Company is finding difficulty in meeting its commitment in connection with the export of coal to Japan under contracts already signed, because the circumstances in which its miners are required to live are not satisfactory to those miners.
Situations of this kind will certainly not be corrected by the prospect offered in Bill C-259. In addition, there are exploration and development expenses which are normally incurred in the vicinity of a mine after it comes into operation-expenses which are required in order to keep
October 22, 1971

a company operating efficiently. Items of this kind should be classified as qualifying for earned depletion allowance. I have been advised that land costs can sometimes amount to 40 per cent of the cost of an oil well. If such costs do not qualify for depletion it can easily be seen that the net tax which is to be paid by these companies will be substantially increased. Indeed, it may no longer be possible for companies to locate and develop these resources.
People in Ontario, particularly in southern Ontario, as well as in other metropolitan areas have a peculiar view about the development of this country. They seem to think we can build up a great number of labour-intensive undertakings overnight. They do not realize that many parts of this country possess only raw materials and that you cannot make labour-intensive employment out of resources of that kind. We must develop these resources because in many areas there is nothing else to develop. It will bear repetition to point out that over the next short period there will be a requirement of $25 billion for the development of the petroleum and natural gas industries to meet the demands presently foreseen, of which only $17 billion will be available from internal sources.

speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but I must remind him that his time has expired.
Continue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member may continue if he has the unanimous consent of the committee. Is there such consent?
Agreed.

I thank the committee for its indulgence in allowing me to conclude my remarks.
In summary, may I say this legislation is not applicable to the problem we are facing today. It appears to me to be part of a grand design to narrow our association with the United States, which will only be to the detriment of both countries. This measure at this particular time will cause untold hardships to the people of Canada, and I urge the government to change its view. Instead of taking the time of the House with this legislation, I urge the government to deal with something that will give new confidence to the people of Canada and put them back to work. That is what is required today.

The trouble is that you always go on to make a long speech, just to mislead us.
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
The hon.
member is tempting me to do what is often done, namely, to say that one will be brief and then to go on for the full time allowed by the rules, but I refuse to be tempted. The reason we of this party have not been in this debate today is the fact that an agreement has been made under which, starting Monday, we shall deal with specific areas and subject matters of the bill. My understanding is that at four o'clock today it is to be agreed that the general discussion is over and that from here on we shall deal with specific matters.
Therefore, since the Minister of Finance gave notice today of the omnibus amendment that he is moving to clause 1, and since on Monday we shall be dealing with the proposed section 109 I should like to give notice that during the course of that discussion we should like to see a change made respecting the main phase of this new, proposed section.
What this section does in the main is to set the new exemption levels of $1,500 for a single taxpayer and $2,850 for a married taxpayer. We have pointed out time and time again that 22 years have elapsed since the present levels of $1,000 and $2,000 were set. We do not thing that the change that has been proposed is at all sufficient.
We also think that consideration should be given to a system of tax credits as perhaps an even better way to provide exemptions for those in the lower income brackets, and we shall be making proposals along this line on Monday. We hope that the government will give consideration to this matter over the weekend. The government knows the arguments that can be'made in favour of this proposal and it knows how weak is the case for this $1,500 and $2,850 set-up. On Monday we hope we can make a real improvement to this section of the bill.
If we also get to the proposed new section 110, when we have finished our discussion on section 109, this section will deal with a number of matters that are allowed as deductions and we think amendments should be made to it too, particularly to the benefit of those in the lower tax brackets.
I hope those hon. members across the way will agree with me that my remarks have been brief. In fact, I have not made a speech; I have simply given notice that on Monday we want some real action by way of changing the proposed exemption levels in this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I enjoyed the remarks of the previous speaker. I took him literally and did not think he meant exactly what he said. For my part, I do not look forward to Monday because when we come to deal with this bill clause by clause, in view of the number of clauses I see no end to it. Quite frankly, I do not think there will be an end to this bill even if the government makes substantial amendments.
Having listened to the discussion so far on clause 1, it seems to me that as Canadians, not only as Members of Parliament, we are being confronted with something that we have not encountered at least within the memories of those of us who are debating this bill. Quite frankly, we are confronted with a new relationship between Canada and the United States and I do not think the Canadian people recognize this. We are hearing more about it every day in the papers of the nation, on radio and television,
