and we are even hearing about it from the people we represent.
I hope hon. members opposite will take this question seriously. As Canadians we have been proud, as have the citizens of the United States, to have the longest undefended border in the world. Suddenly we are made aware of the fact that the United States is now defending that border, at least in economic terms. I am very glad to see that finally some of the minister's advisers are listening to what is said.
What has brought about this sudden confrontation between Canada and the United States? Are we to blame the Minister of Finance? I do not think so. Perhaps the blame lies with the minister's advisers who are advising him to bring forward this bill. In the first place, its provisions are now out of date and, secondly, it does not meet present-day needs. I could detail other deficiencies but time is short. It may be these deficiencies stem from the fact the leader of the government is confronting the United States, first in our relationship with NATO and second in our relationship with NORAD. I see that the Minister of National Defence is paying no attention. The United States has suddenly begun to defend its economic border. I urge the advisers of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to realize that something is wrong.
If you look at the record of the past few weeks, and indeed of the past few years, you will see that there is every evidence that something has gone wrong with regard to Bill C-259. There is a great deal of evidence to show that the bill should be withdrawn. It is not only doing wrong to Canadian taxpayers and the country as a whole; it is creating a wrong impression for the best friend that Canada ever had. It takes two to have that sort of friendship. I am very disturbed at what is apparent today in Canada-U.S. relations and about the effects of Bill C-259. The cause of this trouble may lie with government advisers, the Prime Minister or the leadership of this country. I am not too sure.
When we attempt to deal with this bill clause by clause we will be lost in a real fog; therefore, I urge the leader of this country and his advisers to withdraw the bill and bring forward a new one without delay.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand there is agreement to finish in an orderly way within a few minutes and demonstrate a slight degree of progress. I want to deal with a matter that was raised in this debate the other night by the hon. member for Skeena. As reported at page 8865 of Hansard, he referred to the Atlantic Sugar Refineries Company, Limited. I will paraphrase his words. He said they were bilking, or cheating the Canadian taxpayers out of $2,300,000 because of certain action that would be taken in a few days at a shareholders' meeting. I am not taking up the hon. member in too serious a way. I just want to take this opportunity to put forward the other side of the story.
I thought the hon. member was just using a newspaper clipping to make a point in the debate. In the question period today he pressed the matter further; therefore, I feel I have to go further. Today he asked if one of the ministers of the Crown was investigating this bilking, or

cheating of Canadian taxpayers out of the sum of money I have stated. In a supplementary question I asked if the minister would report and give assurance that this action was nothing more than an ordinary corporate arrangement that would go forward with the full approval of the shareholders.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: You mean they all do it?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, of course, is of the same socialist ilk. I do not mind standing here and defending a company that employs thousands of people in a very honourable and legitimate way.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I say to the hon. member and those in his party that if this company is not allowed to go forward in the proper way and amalgamate its losses, thousands of jobs will be lost. The members of that party will be the first to irresponsibly get up and holler and yell because something was not done about it. This company has been a very good citizen of New Brunswick, through its president, W. J. R. Paton. It has always taken part in community activities in Saint John and, in a larger sphere, in the province of New Brunswick. As everyone knows, it is in difficulty with Acadia Pulp and Paper Limited because of international actions and actions of this government with regard to the dollar. I will not even get into an argument about confidence in the pulp and paper industry. This company also had bad luck with its tuna company which it established anew. It did a very honourable job in this industry in New Brunswick until the difficulties with mercury.
I merely wish to state, on this Friday afternoon, that as far as I am concerned this company is going ahead in the proper way, a way in which it is entitled to go under the law. It has called shareholders' meetings. I suppose they will amalgamate the various companies and in this way consolidate their losses. I hope they will be able to continue their business in New Brunswick. It means thousands of jobs in that province.
Four o'clock.

speechtext: Before I call it four o'clock, having in mind the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is it the understanding of the Chair that the general discussion is now concluded and that on Monday the committee will move to discussion of the details of clauses 109 and 110?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Agreed.
